title: Forgiveness close
hook: sixty days on the hardest gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, different answers: return, grace, mercy, release, reciprocity. Your line was kept whole, in its own words. Did you read your sentence again? Today, the last day of this block on forgiveness. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

A brother runs down a road toward the twin who cheated him. Genesis says it plainly, in the King James words: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." That was early in this block. Since then we've stood with a guard who reached out his hand, a bedtime prayer, a Jain phrase sent wide, a day of fasting, and a long list of people who are hard to forgive. Sixty days on what this path called the hardest gift. Today we gather it up, and then we do the one thing the whole block has been circling: let one thing go.
screen: `ESAU RUNS.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON THE HARDEST GIFT.` → `LET ONE THING GO.`

segments.voice: First, what forgiveness isn't. We drew those lines in the middle of the block. Forgiving is not excusing: the wrong stays named as a wrong. It isn't the same as reconciling, which takes two people and happens only where it's safe. And not yet is allowed. Second, the order. A Jewish teaching said that for wrongs between people, you go to the person first. Jesus told the one bringing a gift to leave it at the altar and be reconciled first. A good apology, we said, owns the wrong and repairs it. Third, the stories. Joseph wept aloud before his brothers. Esau ran. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at Ta'if, did not curse the town that drove him out. Angulimala stopped. Each one is a picture of something held, and a hand that opens. Fourth, the times set aside: the Days of Awe and Yom Kippur, Kshamavani, Forgiveness Sunday, the Night of Power, and the small nightly prayer before sleep. And yesterday's five answers, each kept in its own home. So what does let it go mean, after all that? It doesn't mean the thing was fine. It doesn't mean forgetting, or going back. It means you stop carrying it everywhere you go. Paul's letter to the Colossians puts it in the King James words: "forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any". A quarrel is real. And it can still be set down.
screen: `NOT EXCUSING. NOT ALWAYS RETURNING.` · `THE PERSON FIRST.` · `A HAND THAT OPENS.` · `THE TIMES SET ASIDE.` · then, large: `LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing you've been carrying: small is fine, and small is wise for today. A comment. A slight. A grudge with no one left to argue with. See it clearly, once. Name it, silently, as what it was. Now rest one hand, palm up, on your knee, as if the thing were sitting there. Breathe out slowly, and on the out breath, let the hand relax a little more. You aren't saying it was okay. You're putting it down for the length of this sit. If you pray, you can offer it in your own way. If it comes back, notice that, and set it down again. The bell holds the time.
Quarrel. Paul's word in Colossians for the real complaint that forbearing and forgiving can still set down. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. If the thing you set down comes back today, and it may, say the line and open your hand again. Tomorrow, a new question: awe. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some traditions mark forgiveness with a gesture of release, such as casting crumbs into water at Tashlich, asking forgiveness aloud at Kshamavani, or a bedtime prayer that forgives the day.
